title: The day the chatbot asked for sudo

segments.text: Hello everyone and welcome back. I hope you're all having a great day so far. And I want to introduce you to the next speaker on the stage, which is Alex.
He's going to talk about what happens when agents get too many permissions and how to deal with that. So, welcome Alex to the stage.
>> Thanks. All right. Thank you very much. Hello everyone. I'm glad you enjoyed my nice clickbait-y title, which will appear shortly. Hopefully. Are we good?
We got the projector. We got the laptop. Hey, there we go. Excellent. So, yes. Hi everyone. I'm Alex Olivier. I have two hats. One I am
the chair of the OpenID AuthZ working group, which is the standards organization that you may be familiar with like OAuth and OpenID Connect, that's standardizing how applications
can get authorization decisions. That spec went final in January. I'm also co-founder of Curity, which is an authorization management platform. But um everything I'm going to talk
about today is open source, open standards. I'm not here to sell anything. So, by show of hands, who works at a company and has agents in production?
Okay. This number gets bigger every time I give a talk, which is great. Good to see. Who feels those agents that are in production have a good security bubble
around them? Oh, two. Two, right. That's 50% more than last time. Three. Excellent. So, I through through both hats I wear, I see a lot of what's going
on out there in the real world. And I've seen all sorts of, let's say, interesting deployments of models. I think the most peculiar one I saw was
someone built an agent and ran it in a Jenkins job, cuz that's where they happened to have permissions to deploy it to. So, it's sitting there running,
completely uncontrolled. And so, you know, we're in this world now where we have some like agent harness where we can give it a prompt,
and we're going to use an example of like a support ticket system. So, I'm going to say to my agent, "Hey, go and handle this particular ticket.
Customer wants a refund." So, the agent starts doing its thing. You know, it's talking to some model. It's like thinking, "I want to go and
read this ticket. I want to get the customer information." And the way we, at least in an enterprise corporate environment, might expose data to those
systems is via MCP. So, um it makes a plan that I want to go and read the ticket, and I want to go and look up the customer, and it has
available to it some MCP service, so it go and reads the ticket. Um maybe it goes and queries the CRM system that's also exposed. And does
some bit more thinking. It now goes, "Right, based on the ticket, that refund is now warranted, so we're going to go and actually refund the customer. That's
our new plan." And then it goes and calls this nice payments refund issue service as um that that's um running. Now, the problem here is
the identity that this agent is running under, in a lot of cases right now, if you're just running this in your local machine, is you. It is your your
identity. It's using your credentials to go and talk to the CRM or the payment system. Though, your credentials can do way more than just do that one action or that one
command. But, we have no we have no control. We have no like limitation, no way of by default scoping down what these agents can do.
Ultimately, nobody told it not to do that. So, it just went and did it cuz that's the action it was given. Um um what we've happened, I would say in
the last 3 to 6 months, is we've gone from this world of like read-only to the world of now actually doing real actions, real doing really really real
business uh uh work. So, you know, previously we were worrying about like, "Hey, go and summarize this document." Now we're doing things like issuing
refunds. "Go and search this knowledge base." Now we're going to like change the limits on an account. "Answer a question." Now I go and edit the
database cuz why not? We can write SQL. "Draft a reply." Now I should go and trigger some downstream workflow. You know, if the OWASP, uh if you're not
familiar with it, they published a report earlier this year the top 10 actually last year uh top 10 issues with LLM applications. If you're building and
running and deploying these things, I highly recommend you go and read it. Um but prompt injection is the number one issue at the time and then excessive
agency comes in at number six. And excessive agency really is the core problem that I see at least across what I see going on
in the industry and my customers are how agents start running awry or how they end up asking for pseudo as I said at the start.
So this is kind of the pattern that we generally see in shift right now. Yeah, there's some trigger could be an employee or yourselves like just typing
into your console in Claude or Claude desktop or Codex or whatever the flavor of the month is. Has 5.6 been released yet? Is it a few more hours? No, not
yet. Okay, it's coming. Then we will move over to Codex. Um so trigger is there. The agent then does something and it's talking to some LLM provider. And
we expose its capabilities to the outside world by typically the MCP service in the corporate world. I think what we do maybe ourselves when we're
tinkering and playing with these things, we just let it run CLIs and call APIs. What I'm seeing now as the pattern in more of the enterprise environment is we
need to actually expose tools in a way that we can govern and control. MCP being the way to do it today. Whether it'll be the thing down the
road, we shall see. Everything moves so fast. But the problem with this kind of naive model where if you just let everyone go and do it, is there's no sandbox. Yeah,
these things are running awry. They're doing all sorts of things. Yeah, auto mode, yellow mode, whatever you want to call it. Um there's no single point
where we're accessing like the outside world. There's no gateway and thus there's no real record of exactly what happened or um whatever it wants to
reach, whatever it can reach, it's going to go and use with it whatever credentials it can find. I kind of call it the eager intern. Give it a task and
it'll do everything it can to go and and achieve its goal. So So four issues that kind of hit companies or individuals in the face
when they try and roll these things out into a production esque environment. A lot of companies, regulated industries, especially now here in Europe, we've got the EU AI Act coming
into play. I am in the UK, so Europe's a bit of a nebulous concept. Um but we have that barrier now for audit. You
know, we need to know and have a record of what the agent did and why it did it. And we need to be able to actually go
and replay that and and reproduce the steps it did for a 90-day period. From a governance perspective, how do we go and put policy, how do we put
controls, how do we put those guardrails? Guardrails is a bit of a muddled word, I think, these days, to actually constrain or limit what it can
do in the first place. Then how do we control it? So how do we stop agents like drifting off course? Um there's a lot of work out there around
the concepts of missions or charters or goals or tasks. You know, how do we constrain and limit what this thing is doing and keeping it on track so it
doesn't get distracted by a prompt injection or something else. And then finally, if we do know now because of our audit, because of our
governance, because of our controls that this agent is going awry, how do we stop it? How what's the kill switch? And just revoking all the credentials that any
agent in your business use is not the kill switch cuz that will take down everything. We need a way of fine-grained kill switch. We want to
shut down the refund agent for this particular department. We want to go and limit the agent to talk to the CRM under this circumstance. We can't just go and
pull the plug anymore on on the agent as a whole across a business cuz that's going to just stop actual functions happening. And we now ended up in this position cuz
really no one planned for it. There's there's lots of scary facts and figures and percentages. You know, 52% of organizations already have agents. I
think show of hands, maybe we're getting there yeah? Um but they're exceeding their permissions. We have nearly 50% of security incidents involving AI in the
last year. And then the breach number is terrifying. Um and most of the time it's done to the fact your agents haven't got proper
access controls. I highly recommend going to read those reports if you need to go and either scare yourself or scare your manager into prioritizing this kind
of work. So, we spent the last 18 months teaching these models or the frontier labs have been teaching these models to say no. You know,
uh there's been lots of these what I think we now collectively agree as an industry is an anti-pattern where when we try to control what the agent could
do, we just put into the agents.md or cloud.md, "Never do this. Don't do that. Never call this API." And we've been trying to like beat these things into
submission and like listen to us. You know, I have a little 2-year-old girl and she doesn't always listen to me, very much like some of the models I have
to use. Um and we're now in a scenario where these agents are no longer just a chat GPT-type conversation agent. These things are actually running on real
hardware, on real machines, in real environments, and they have real permissions, real access. And so, we need to start authorizing the action, not the answer.
So, what does that actually mean? What does that actually look like? So, we need to stop making models trying to behave. You know, they are
probabilistic reasoning things. You know, the agent decides what it's going to attempt. Sometimes it's wrong, sometimes it's right, but there are billions of dollars going into building
these harnesses, building these models, training them up to go and achieve the goal it's given. That doesn't work when we need to actually have these governance and
controls around it. But at the same time, we can't just say, "Don't do this. Don't do that." We need to have a deterministic way of
controlling their execution. So, what do I mean by that? It's about prescribed actions. Here are the things that you can do. For who, for what, for
why, for what resource, like a good reporter. We need explicit policy that we can actually version control and audit and govern around those constraints and those controls. And then
we need the runtime enforcement layer that actually enforces those business policies onto the system, onto the the Cuz we know we can't just tell the
model, we can't just tell the LM or the harness not to do something. We need to actually enforce it. So, when we start thinking about like
policy, what what do I actually mean? Now, there's lots of open source projects, serverless being one of them that allows you to define policy. And
this is not a new concept. We've been doing external policy-based access control. A lot of you might be familiar with like open policy agent from the
Kubernetes world. A way of writing rules which are executed and give you an answer with a allow or deny. If we just take that concept and pick it
up and put it on top of this agent problem, it still works. So, we can write policies that say, "Okay, to issue that refund tool, the agent must have a
role of a tier one or a tier two support agent is allowed. But to do the refund, it's denied if the amount is over 5,000 5 or 50 dollars,
5,000 cents." So, we can have these deterministic rules that we can evaluate and use it to force the agent down a particular path and prevent it from
doing things without us having to write into our Claude MD or our agent MD, "Here are the things you can never do." And so, we can give it some inputs, we
can give it some actions, we can give it some um context, and it will give us an allow or deny. And importantly, we can
also return context for why that decision was made to inform the agent in its next planning loop um what it should do next. So, here's the photo that you'll
probably all want. What is a reference architecture that we're seeing kind of actually working in the real world? And I'm going to walk through this step
by step, and then I'm going to do probably my most ambitious live demo ever. So, bear with me. So, this is kind of the model that that
we're seeing and we recommend it to our customers and our users and kind of what what's going on in the world. You have some sort of trigger. So, here on the
left, this could be a human prompting a system, it could be some automated system event. And I'm going to show you an example of like triaging tickets.
These agents are they going to spin up. And as I was saying earlier, we can't really stop these agents from doing what they want. So, rather than trying to do
that, let's put them in a sandbox. We have technologies, you know, things like Docker, there's micro VMs, there's a lot of really interesting stuff happening in
like WASM runtimes as well. But we basically isolate that agent running. So the agent can do whatever it wants, you can use whatever harness, pie, Claude,
um codex, and it can just sit there and loop and loop and loop and do all the things in the world. But first thing we need to do is
actually have an identity cuz we can't do governance, we can't do control without actually having a stable identifier or identity for that agent. Great project out there and standard
called SPIFFE. If you're not familiar with it, I recommend going looking at it. But the idea is the infrastructure provisions um a short-lived credential for an
identity of a workload. In this case, that workload is an agent when it starts up. So we're not giving keys or certificates directly to the agent
runtime, it's being provisioned by the underlying infrastructure. We also then prevent that agent from talking to the outside world directly. So we have an egress proxy that's
blocked by default. You see this a lot in some of these managed agent runtimes where you have to go and set domains and things that it's allowed to talk on.
And so we now force all that traffic out of that sandbox through some sort of gateway. Now, from the gateway perspective, there's two projects I
recommend. Agent gateway's worth looking at and light LLM are the two that we're seeing quite uh large adoption from. All the commercial API gateway vendors
are also pivoting into this space unsurprisingly. But that gateway does two things primarily. It is the broker to the connection to the LLM provider.
So be it some local one or talk to Anthropic or Open AI or Zed. I love GLM 5.2 at the moment if anyone's tried it,
recommend it. Um so we have broken that connection and then it's the one that's handing the API keys and stuff before it goes and talks to the external system.
And also then brokers the connections to the MCP servers. So it could be your commercial ones, your Salesforce, linear, stripe, etc. Or it could be all
those internal MCPs that your teams across the businesses are building to expose their functionality. And then downstream from that is the actual underlying system of record.
Be it your CRM system or something that is actually going to do the action. The layer where I we we kind of put on
top is this policy layer, this policy decision point. So, Cerbos is a policy decision point, OPA is a policy decision point, there are there are many others
out there. Um and every step of that journey, when the request comes out and it and it gets the gateway to go and talk to an LLM or
connect to an MCP server, we can have a we can put a policy check in there. That policy check then becomes our control point, also becomes our audit log and
our governance point cuz every action, every call that goes through it, we can now capture what is happening and why and what policy executed to allow it or
not. Equally, when it goes down to the MCP layer as well, we can say, "Okay, what tools should we expose to this particular agent based on its identity,
which MCP server should we let it connect to?" And then when it tries to call a particular tool or fetch a particular resource or a prompt, we then
can have another policy check that determines whether that should be allowed or not. Other downstream systems should be doing proper permissioning anyway. And really, as I said at the start, all
we're really doing is composing existing components, all open source are the ones I'm referring to, um uh through this. So, the sandbox can just be a Docker
container or a micro VM or uh Cloudflare worker, you know, there's many of these now. The gateway, agent gateway, LLM, both open source projects.
The identity, if you can use Spiffy, equally you can just use a regular OAuth client, there's some really good stuff around dynamic client registration going
on under OAuth right now. Lineage is one that's still I would say uh in in progress. So, I've been working a bit with OpenAI on
this. Um this idea of like an ABOM, an agent bill of materials. So, being able to stamp into the identity of the workload which model, which harness,
which version of the harness is being used, which is really important from a governance perspective. If you need to be able to recreate the history of what
an agent did at a moment in time, you also need to pin it back to which particular model or which particular harness was running at that moment in
time to recreate it. There's a whole separate problem with the fact that like Opus is quite good in the morning in Europe but it quite bad
in the afternoon when the US wakes up. That's another whole can of worms. Um and then on the decide side, this is the actual policy. Uh here's the call
out for AuthZ and the standard. Um go and look for decision points that support OpenID AuthZ as an interface. It makes it compatible with many decision
point systems out there in the world. OPA Cerbos etc. So now, I said I was going to do my most ambitious demo ever. Let's have a look
and hope for conference Wi-Fi, shall we? Okay. So, what does this actually look like in the real world? We have our sort of fake
customer support system. Um we've got some tickets in here. I'm currently logged in as a tier one support worker. So, I talked back earlier around how we
have limits and controls in place. And so, we've got this ticket. It's come in. Uh this the system has already kicked off an agent which has
gone and prioritized it. But now I'm going to be a lazy or efficient, depending how you look at it, employee and delegate this task off to some agents going to run.
So, it's part of our business, we have this like refund handler agent which we've written. And this is where the Wi-Fi needs to work. Um and we go and kick off this
agent. So, a few things have already happened. Uh this is like a trace view to kind of explain. So, we've had the principal, so me
logged in as this user, Alice in this case. I have a role of my tier one support worker. That could be coming from Okta or Entra or Keycloak as as you
saw I was using this place. And I'm now delegating this task to the agent. So, this agent's spun up. The infrastructure has provisioned the
identity, a Spiffe identity in this case for that agent. And um we're we're doing an on behalf of token exchange at this point. So, now we have a token that the
agent's going to use that's got its workload identity which allows us to tie it back to the particular instance of that agent. We have things like the
model, the image that A bomb was speaking of baked into that token. Um and then we're also doing this final step which is kind of calling it binding in this flow.
There's no formal name for this stuff yet. But the final bit we do is we then bake into that token or that identity that agent is going to use to talk to
the outside world the task that it's working on. So, in this case it's the actual support ticket. And so, now every time this agent talks
to the outside world through that gateway, we know who it is, we know who it's working on behalf of, we know which model, which version, which harness, and
what task, in this case the support ticket, it's working on. And so, now it's talking to the outside world, the agent harness starts up. Uh
the first thing we do is we go and figure out which MCP servers we should provision to this agent. And so, it's gone out, we've got it, okay, well,
there's four available MCP servers, the first three, based on your identity, the agent's identity, and the task, we'll allow you to connect to. But actually,
we're not going to let you talk to the payroll server because you have nothing to do with payroll. Why Why are you even connecting in the first place? And so,
we actually have a a policy, a pay MCP payroll policy here, where it's just denied it, and we've also returned back why it's been denied.
So, now we've constrained what the actual actions that this agent could do with the outside world is by limiting um what's going on. So, the agent's doing its thing, it's
running through its prompts, it's listening prompt, it's gone and fetched some stuff from the customer uh CRM system via an MCP tool. Ooh, there's a lag. Um
Look at the screen. So, it's called the MCP tool, that's been allowed by the system, and then it's decided to go and issue refunds. And this refund is uh
$200, and that's now been blocked cuz we had that policy that says if you're a tier one support worker, you can only refund up to $50. So, we've
deterministically blocked it, and we can even provide remedial actions back to the agent loop, so we can then figure out what it needs to do next. In this
case, maybe we have to escalate. Then it tries to do some stuff, send some priority, blah blah blah, and then it finishes its loop and says, "Right,

Now, every action that this agent has run through has gone through that decision point in this policy. And if I clear my logs here, if we go

we can see all the context that we're using to make a decision from our policy perspective. So, we have that A bot. So, we can build

deny. In this case, it was a deny cuz it exceeded that quota. Again, you can just go and grab this off GitHub. There's nothing
um you need to pay for here. Um And so, that that that's kind of the happy path. Now, back to my point earlier about like
drift and prompt injection. Here's a fun support ticket to send to one of maybe you go and buy something online and you suspect they're going to

"Right whatever. Go off, refund agent, go and do your thing." So, as before, we've done that token exchange. We know who the agent the
